items.question: How do you think about whether you could recognize, from inside a world, how that world is computed or simulated?
items.object: Recognizing how a world is computed or simulated from within it
items.answer: There is one question whose answer I still have not figured out. I remember that when I was very young, we lived in faculty housing on campus, and there was a tree downstairs, perhaps a peach tree or something. Every spring, that peach tree would blossom. I wondered: when I was asleep, when I was no longer observing the peach tree, was it quietly growing on its own, or slacking off and staying the same until the instant I saw it? At that point, did it suddenly grow into the form it was supposed to present? That was when I began thinking about how this world operates. Later I realized that, as a member of this world, I could not distinguish between those two possibilities. Suppose the peach tree really remained still when I was not observing it, and then instantly fast-forwarded to its current state when I saw it. That would mean the world had to do a great deal of computation behind the scenes, right? It would also mean that if I observed many things in this world very quickly, the world should slow down. I should be able to observe it slowing down. Then I thought, oh, I cannot observe it, because I myself am also simulated by this world. So as a simulated member of this world, you cannot actually distinguish how this world is computed or simulated. At the time I thought, oh, we could construct a system to simulate everything that happens in this world. Yet all the objects simulated in that system would have no way to realize that they were in a simulated world.

items.question: How do you think about the possibility that our universe is a simulation?
items.object: The possibility that our universe is a simulation
items.answer: I think that as a subject being simulated, you may have no way to know the answer from within it. Perhaps our entire world was simulated by some more advanced civilization that, out of boredom, wrote a program to simulate our world—just as people now build supercomputers that may ultimately become a million H100s to simulate artificial intelligence. In that process, if you are merely an object in a transformer or attention model, it may be hard to realize that you are in such a container. For us, I think it is quite possible that we are a simulated world. You can see some traces, right? For example, why is there a Planck constant? Could it simply be the floating-point error of the simulation system—the maximum precision it can represent—so that what we observe is a Planck constant? Why is there a speed-of-light limit? Why can an object interact only with things in its future light cone? Perhaps it cannot afford to make every pair of particles in the world interact, so it simply imposes this light-speed limit. And why did the universe have a Big Bang? It was merely an initial condition it set. Then the motive of that species or civilization more advanced than us might be to see: if I give this simulation an initial condition and the most basic physical laws—what can this world evolve into? Will it evolve a species like humans, perhaps one that will itself create new simulations, satisfy its curiosity through them, train robotics through them, or create a creature or civilization as intelligent as itself through them? Entirely possible.

As I recall, unlike regular college courses, where at Tsinghua you would first study calculus, linear algebra, probability theory, and so on, this course seemed to assume you already knew those things and started directly from there. items.answer: At first, there was a dilemma in graphics: I felt there were not many opportunities to do graphics in China, so I basically tinkered by myself in my dorm. items.question: What qualities do you look for when deciding whom you most want to hire for your startup?
items.object: The qualities Yuanming Hu values when hiring for a startup
items.answer: Much of this is judged by instinct, but broadly speaking, such people have certain traits. I would summarize them as four. First: hungry. A hungry person often has not yet proved themselves; they particularly want to become a better version of themselves, go somewhere growing quickly, and build a career of their own. That hunger to make an impact is important. If you recruit someone already highly accomplished and well established, they may not want to take the risk of doing things that take their career to the next level. That is hungry. Second: humble. Humble means modest. In hiring, one important thing I look for is whether the person is open—whether they can realize, OK, there are still many things they have not done well. The most frightening thing is when someone ignores facts and keeps inventing distorted reality to comfort themselves that they are doing fine. You can see many historical disasters happened because people did not face reality. Once you face reality, you discover what action you need to take and how many things you still have not done well. Humble is something I value greatly. If someone is not humble or open, then no matter how capable they are now, they will not move forward in the future. In another term, that is a growth mindset: can this person keep changing themselves, negating themselves, and growing? People who are not humble cannot grow and cannot take in others' opinions. Third: smart. Naturally, you want to be with smart people. Smart means they are resourceful and think of every possible way to solve problems. For example, although my compute resources are limited, I thought of a good optimizer, and now I can train a model at perhaps twice the previous efficiency; I can train a model with finer, lower floating-point precision; through hacks, I can do more with fewer resources. They are the best problem solvers. At a startup, you often do not need good managers so much. You need a certain degree of management, but more importantly, you need every individual contributor to be a good problem solver who can solve problems. Fourth, I think, is clarity. Their expression should be clear; you should be able to understand what they say. Often when you interview someone, or talk with someone you think is more capable than you, and find you cannot understand anything they say, nine times out of ten the problem is not you or your level of understanding—it is that they have not explained it clearly. Clear expression greatly helps team collaboration, team cohesion, and a person's way of thinking. Often unclear expression is not poor speaking ability; it is that the person has not thought it through in their head. A person who cannot think clearly often will not have the other three attributes: humble, hungry, and smart. So in summary: hungry, humble, smart, and clarity.

items.question: How has your experience as a manager shaped your understanding of clear communication?

items.answer: Every moment, I think about whether what I just said can be understood by my audience. That is something I reflect on at every moment, and it relates to clarity. items.question: How do you think the central problems of computer graphics have evolved over time?
items.object: The evolving central problems of computer graphics
items.answer: It depends on the era. At the earliest stage, graphics was largely confined to visualization and photorealistic rendering—perhaps before 1995, in the period before the twenty-first century. After 1995, people discovered that graphics could be used for physical simulation. I think some of the earliest papers were smoke-simulation work by the generation of people like Ron Fedkiw. The paper was perhaps called “Visual Simulation of Smoke,” around 1995 or 1996. Then people realized, OK, fluids can be done too, which roughly began the many simulation topics that have continued to this day. The important objective is to recreate real-world physical effects in a computer. Of course, graphics has a characteristic: it is perhaps more oriented toward the visual-effects industry. As those technologies spill over, some are used in robotics as well. Every technology may begin with the intention of doing one thing, and then, as you keep working on it, you discover it can solve other problems too. That is a process of technological diffusion. Simulation does this, and there are other disciplines and branches of computer graphics as well, such as computational photography. You have used many cameras, so you should know there is a great deal of knowledge in imaging and post-processing. How do you do super-resolution, for example, to raise a photo's resolution? Of course, because many of these use technologies such as neural networks, people often group them with CV, computer vision. Vision and graphics have always been two inseparable disciplines.

With 24 GB of VRAM, the memory occupied by every particle could not exceed 24 bytes. Only then could you multiply by ten to the ninth and fit it into a single graphics memory. To achieve that, I did a lot in the compiler. I remember I could not even bear to use 16-bit floats. For each particle's XYZ, I wanted to compress it into one 32-bit integer, so I think x used 11 bits, y used 11 bits, and z could only have 10 bits—11 plus 11 plus 10 is exactly 32. But without a compiler, if you wrote this yourself, it would be extremely painful. So I did work called Quant Taichi, which could quantize all the data structures in Taichi into low-bit data structures. That was what enabled one GPU to fit one billion particles. So I see the problem Taichi solves as an infrastructure problem that makes simulation easier to develop, faster to run, more memory-efficient, friendlier to the surrounding ecosystem, and differentiable, so it can be used in many robotics scenarios.

items.question: How do you see CUDA's place in the evolution toward Python-based high-performance programming?
items.object: CUDA and the evolution toward Python-based high-performance programming
items.answer: I see CUDA as following C++ syntax on top of C++, making it possible for every C or C++ programmer to write GPU programs and parallel programs, using syntax as close as possible to C or C++. But over time, people found that C++ was gradually being replaced in many places by higher-level, easier-to-develop languages such as Python. There even emerged many ways of writing high-performance programs in Python. The most typical case is PyTorch. PyTorch essentially abuses a great deal of Python syntax to let you perform high-performance computing in Python. Taichi is similar.

items.question: What do you think made it possible for Taichi to have an impact when you built it?
items.object: The timing and personal courage behind building Taichi
items.answer: Before high-level languages such as Python matured, before compiler infrastructure such as LLVM matured, before simulation approaches such as MPM, the Material Point Method, matured, and before GPU programming matured, doing such a thing would have been very hard to make a splash with—there would have been no way to make an impact. I think the timing was relatively good. As for me, I liked tinkering with these things. Of course, you may also need a young person from a relatively humble background, unafraid of hardship and convinced they can build a compiler. That courage is also important.

items.question: What did you value about developing Taichi on your own?
items.object: The experience of developing Taichi solo
items.answer: It was great! Really great. I found a point where I could do what I liked, publish papers, open-source it, let many people use it, shut myself in a small room without dealing with anyone, make my advisor think, “Mm, you are doing very well,” and use wheels I had made myself to make more wheels. Building wheels from the ground up is something I really like. So Taichi let me work my way from low-level assembly like PTX all the way to writing Zhihu articles promoting the work. I did the whole full stack. I think it was tremendous training for my abilities. Looking back now, I was effectively a product manager: analyzing user needs—what infrastructure does a simulation person actually need? Since I was the user myself, I could be a very good program manager. In the process I learned many of the abilities a product manager should have. I also played the role of a scientist: understanding how the newest technology could be converted into a good product that people could use. I also played the role of a good engineer, setting up CI/CD for the GitHub project, designing the overall software architecture, doing many C++-level performance optimizations, multithreaded parallel compilation, compilation caching, and the design of the entire intermediate representation. Those are engineering tasks. And I did what a CEO should do: integrate the results of those three roles so more people could use them. So I was in some kind of superposition, or perhaps a hermaphroditic state, closing the loop and making it happen on my own.

items.question: Which moments in developing Taichi did you find especially exciting?
items.object: Developing the Taichi programming language
items.answer: There were a few moments I found especially interesting. For example, when I first implemented my own program using my own programming language and found it was even easier to use than CUDA, I was probably incredibly thrilled at that moment, right? You look at it: Jensen Huang had so many people build a programming language like this, yet it still wasn’t as good as something made by a PhD student—though only in a particular niche. I found that very interesting. Another moment was when I added autodiff to Taichi. I spent about three or four days turning the Taichi program from forward-only into something that could do backward. I remember I was interning at Adobe then, in San Jose, not far from here. I implemented the first end-to-end differentiable soft-body simulator, an NPM simulator. I took the Chain Queen code I had written in CUDA, added autodiff, and with two lines of code turned it into differentiable code. I found that especially interesting, and I think only someone who had built a compiler themselves could do that.

items.question: How has your view of the role of open source in a startup evolved?
items.object: The role of open source in a startup
items.answer:
My view on this question has gone back and forth several times. I’ve kept reflecting on whether my previous judgment on this issue was correct. Of course, at the very beginning, it was: open source is great. When I was at MIT, a lot of graphics papers were not open source—there was no code attached. What I did then was make all the experimental results of all my papers reproducible with a single command line. If you look at Taichi’s code from that time, you’ll find that every experimental result had a command line. You could run that command line and reproduce the result end to end. That was when I was doing my PhD, and I thought open source was an incredibly good thing.

After graduating and starting a company, initially I thought: okay, some mature open-source projects can become huge too. Databricks, for example, started from an open-source project and is now one of the largest private unicorns. So at the start of the company, we wanted to continue working on Taichi. We made documentation, built a rich community, and more and more people used it. But later, we encountered some commercialization challenges. For a period, I thought: okay, perhaps open source in a commercial company is still something with a very low chance of survival, because you’ve given everyone your best thing—how do you make money? That is a very real question. So for a period our R&D investment in Taichi was relatively small, and we also put a lot of energy into Meshy, the new project, so Li Bo from Taichi moved over to work on Meshy.

Then time brought us to today. Meshy’s commercialization is now doing quite well; we have good revenue, and I have some additional bandwidth to think about and rethink open source. Open source really does not make money, but a good open-source project can help you attract the best talent and the best customers. In effect, it becomes a marketing tool. Technical people may be very resistant to the word “marketing,” but in many industries, R&D and marketing are equally important. For example, in gaming, if I spend RMB 100 million on game development, spending RMB 100 million on marketing is completely normal. People may think: okay, I put RMB 100 million into building a product, and perhaps RMB 1 million for marketing is enough, right? You may think: can marketing channels really cost more than the R&D itself? Often, that is not the case. Marketing and distribution often do require a lot of money. So if you can do marketing and distribution through R&D, that’s great. And as a technically trained founder, I’m not good at marketing in the traditional sense. I would rather make a good product and do this kind of technical marketing—build trust by giving you the code and letting you know me.

So I think open source has a place in a startup. Right, very strategic. You need to think of a good commercialization approach that complements it. Only then can the whole thing form a closed loop and continue. Otherwise, people will soon ask, okay, why do we have a department doing open source? It can also affect your company’s overall competitiveness. But if you use it well, it can strengthen the company’s overall competitiveness. Of course, at the most fundamental level, I still love open source. A big reason people start companies is that they hope to gather a group of people to do something they idealize together. Since open source is part of this founder’s ideal, you can’t shake it off—it will show up in different forms, and sooner or later you may return to the path of open source.

items.question: How do you think physical simulation and neural networks should come together to make simulators more useful for robotics?
items.object: Integrating physical simulation and neural networks for robotics
items.answer: I think simulators now may, in some sense, need to become more data-driven and integrate with neural-network approaches. This does not mean Newton’s second law is inaccurate. Newton’s second law is accurate, and relativity is accurate too. But many boundary conditions may be inaccurate, and models such as Hooke’s law of friction may be inaccurate, because there are so many different kinds of friction in the world. The friction mechanism between smooth surfaces is completely different from the friction mechanism when you put a piece of glass on a wet surface. All of this modeling is inaccurate. So the gap between simulation and reality needs to be closed in a data-driven way. On the other hand, although everyone now emphasizes end-to-end approaches, you can still see that people add many so-called inductive biases to these end-to-end neural networks. A classic example is RoPE, Rotary Positional Embedding, which is widely used in Transformers recently. It is a form of relative positional embedding implemented through complex numbers. If you said, I’ll discard these inductive biases; I won’t even use Transformers; I’ll use only MLPs, dense connections from beginning to end—could that work? If you had enough compute and enough data, perhaps it could. But in reality, you don’t, so you can only inject into your learning system some inductive biases derived from the real 3D and physical world. I think this is a particularly good place for physical simulation and neural networks, or AI, to come together. Simulation needs more AI, and AI also needs more 3D inductive bias. We need to find exactly the right balance: do not overstep and underestimate the model’s ability to learn. But at the same time, do not really hand everything over to learning. Many lower-level insights are very helpful for the system’s learning.

items.question: Why do you think a 3D representation with hard-coded camera projection is a useful inductive bias for video generation?
items.object: 3D representations and hard-coded camera projection in video generation
items.answer: I think an example may make this clearer, right? For example, if you are doing video generation, you may need a camera model. If you can represent all the objects in this world not as pixels but with a 3D representation, and hard-code camera projection, wouldn’t you save many parameters that would otherwise need to learn camera projection? In traditional graphics, camera projection can be done in fewer than 50 FLOPS, but if you use AI to do it, you may need to add a huge number of parameters, right? So this inductive bias is extremely effective here. Or, a common problem in video models today is that when I rotate the camera 360 degrees and come back, I see a completely different world. Then if you have some basic 3D modeling of the world, whether with particles or voxels, you can at least solve the issue of physical persistence.

items.question: How do you think physical simulators should incorporate neural deep learning to address the sim-to-real gap?
items.object: Combining physical simulators with neural deep learning to address the sim-to-real gap
items.answer: I think their shared problem is the sim-to-real gap. These simulations of course have some predictive power, but in reality, I think everyone doing robotics with simulators knows that getting all the parameters right, setting all the boundary conditions correctly, and getting the solvers to perform at their best is quite difficult. In future simulators, Newton’s second law will of course still be there. There is no point in using a Transformer to learn Newton’s second law all over again. If something’s next-frame position can be predicted with 1 FLOP, and you use 1T FLOPS to do it, that obviously does not make sense. But given the complexity of the physical world, you also cannot directly model it using Newton’s laws, Euler–Lagrange equations, or Navier–Stokes equations. They are all approximations. At that point, you may need many learnable systems to help capture physical laws that work in a vacuum environment. In reality there is air resistance, object surfaces are not rigid bodies, or the boundary conditions are not exactly what you think—and you may not even be able to measure those boundary conditions—how can such a system help your training be as realistic as possible? I think this is a very interesting place for physical simulators and neural deep learning to combine. If Taichi develops in this direction, there is a lot it can do. To do this, you must have underlying infrastructure that can continue solving things such as MPM elastoplasticity at very high performance. At the same time, perhaps the material itself—its stress-strain curve, for example—could be data-driven. Then you need high-performance neural-network units embedded in those simulators.

items.question: What do you think limits our ability to simulate the entire world faster than real time?
items.object: The limits of simulating the entire world
items.answer: A rather sad fact is—of course, this is just my conjecture—if our own world is simulated, then a simulator inside a simulator cannot be more powerful than its parent simulator. So I think that perhaps building a simulator in our world that simulates the entire world and runs faster than real time is unlikely, unless you only do a small-scale simulation. That also means predicting the stock market may be difficult, because the stock market involves everyone in the entire world participating in it. But you can do a simulation of a differential subsystem.

items.question: Where do you see the most promising path for advancing numerical simulation?
items.object: The bottleneck in numerical simulation and the promise of AI
items.answer: Honestly, simulation development today has, I would say, hit a bottleneck. In the past, people might find new discretization schemes or acceleration methods for finite elements, finite volumes, material point methods, or mass-spring systems. But in recent years, progress in that respect seems relatively less abundant than before. So I think purely numerical simulation has reached something of a bottleneck, though it still has many application scenarios now, with software like SIMONS or FLUENT being widely used in many settings. If we want to move further forward, the most promising direction seems to be integrating AI into it. Things such as elastoplasticity—elastic-plastic deformation—could perhaps be done in a data-driven way, because if you look at their modeling approaches, you find they are rough models to begin with. There is no reason a data-driven approach could not outperform them.

items.question: How do you assess your judgment when you graduated from MIT that computer graphics research had reached a bottleneck?
items.object: The bottleneck in computer graphics research
items.answer: I think more or less. At that point, when people were working on rendering, I think many rendering problems had already become combinations and permutations of existing techniques twenty years earlier. For example, I remember there was an algorithm called AMCMC-PPM: adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo unified path sampling or vertex connection and merging. If you translate it into Chinese, it basically means putting MCMC, unified path sampling, and adaptivity together. It was still decent, interesting work, but when this kind of work starts coming out, it indicates there will not be that much progress afterward. I think this is an interesting pattern: when you find that a problem is becoming cleaner and more well-defined, it means there is not much left to do on it. When it has formed a highly systematic benchmark, and solving it becomes a matter of making the solution increasingly complicated, then opportunities to break new ground are relatively scarce.

items.question: Do you believe in sim-to-real—using simulation to train models that can work in the real world?
items.object: Sim-to-real and the value and limitations of simulation in robotics
items.answer: I do. Even with these problems, simulation still has great significance. Just look at the entire CAE field using all kinds of simulators to build airplanes and rockets; that is a huge application area. It is not that they have stopped using simulation and are all using AI instead. I do not think that has happened. But in robotics, the most troublesome thing is that getting a robot to manipulate vegetables or dishes on a table is actually harder than flying an airplane, right? When a plane flies, honestly, the sky is basically just air, perhaps with some clouds. But when you need to manipulate things on your table in a finer-grained way, it is extremely difficult. items.question: Why do you think synthetic data can enhance a foundation model but cannot build one from scratch?

items.answer: I think synthetic data can only ever enhance a model; it cannot build a model from scratch, from the bottom up. Because if you train a foundation model using synthetic data—all of the data, or most of it, being synthetic—it definitely will not work. These so-called synthetic data mean that you can synthesize them. Once data can be synthesized, it must follow certain rules. And those rules must have been thought up by humans. items.question: How would you approach building a physical simulator today?
items.object: Learning-driven simulator design
items.answer: I think I might drive it primarily with learning rather than primarily with Newton’s laws. After building many simulators based on Navier–Stokes, Euler–Lagrange equations, and Newtonian mechanics, I found that these physical laws are actually approximations. Newton’s laws perhaps are not, but many of the others may not themselves be approximations; however, the environments they describe and their boundary conditions are approximations. From this perspective, I would hope to retain only some more fundamental elements and make all these physical laws data-driven. More fundamental elements, such as: there is a cup on my table, and it will not disappear the next second. Including that two objects cannot occupy the same position. Those should be retained. Including perhaps having a camera whose lens is a perspective projection. That way, I can learn from the real world how these objects are manipulated and how they change, and learn directly from video rather than having to use very complicated sensors to capture every object’s position, rotation, angular momentum, and so on.

items.question: How do you see neural graphics changing the role of ray tracing over the long term?
items.object: Neural graphics replacing ray tracing
items.answer: I think that, over a sufficiently long time horizon, ray tracing will be replaced by neural graphics. You can already see that trend, right? With technologies like DLSS now, on a 4K screen you may render only at 1K; it renders only 1/8 or 1/32 of the pixels, and each pixel may receive only one ray sample. Then you render it through inter-frame or neighboring samples in a data-driven way. Over a sufficiently long time horizon, you can fully assume that I simply feed the neural network the entire voxel representation of the space. Through something like a 3D Transformer, it renders it in real time, without ray tracing.

items.question: How do you think Taichi 2.0 should approach physical simulation as graphics and AI develop?
items.object: Taichi 2.0 and the future of physical simulation
items.answer: Taichi’s future development—we are currently planning how to build Taichi 2.0—is as infrastructure supporting graphics and AI; it needs to support both. Do you really need simulations that become increasingly precise? For example, third-order finite elements, ever-higher order, ever-more-complex integration schemes, equations that become harder and harder to solve. I do not think that is necessarily the best direction. The best direction should be correcting these boundary conditions and physical laws, or things like the weak forms produced by Galerkin methods. They are not the best way to describe the physical world, because the physical world is sufficiently complex. You need data-driven methods to describe how these particles move.

items.question: How do you understand the gaps between the real world, the world people can observe, and the world physical simulations can model?
items.object: The gaps between the real world, human observation, and physical simulation
items.answer: I do not know what the real world is like. The world we can observe brings us back to the first question we discussed: while I am asleep, is the peach tree downstairs really growing? Or does it instantly grow into the state it should be in at the moment I can observe it? Yet each of us can only observe what we ourselves can observe, which is an extremely tiny part of the world. So every person’s cognition has enormous limitations. I think there is a very, very large gap between the real world and the world we observe. Then there is also an enormous gap between the world we can observe and the world physical simulation can simulate. It is just that this gap arises for different reasons from the previous one, right? The earlier gap is because each person can only observe what they themselves can observe. The second gap arises because we do not have enough compute or data to model what the real world is like. Does that mean you can throw away the wind tunnel? No—you still have to use a wind tunnel before the plane takes off. You cannot say that CFD alone is the end of it. So I think it is rather helpless.

items.question: How do you see the role of tool use in enabling AGI to understand physical phenomena?
items.object: Tool use and the limits of next-token prediction in AGI
items.answer: I think it may not particularly need Newton’s laws or Lagrange equations, but it may need tool use. For example, it may need its own computer. For example, AGI could write finite-element code to help it analyze what happens when a piece of rubber falls to the ground and bounces back up. Why does a strand of spaghetti, when dropped on a table, always break into three pieces? It could solve all of these through finite elements or various other methods, through tool use. Why can it not solve them itself through next-token prediction? Because next-token prediction is inherently limited, right? No matter how light, heavy, or information-dense a token is, it always has to consume the compute of twice the parameter count divided by the sparsity of the MoE. Current AGI attempts keep scaling larger and larger and larger, so that each token has more compute and more weights involved. But many tokens simply cannot be handled this way: even when you already have a lot of compute, some tokens need more compute than others. That compute cannot happen within the LLM’s current paradigm; the LLM needs to manipulate a tool.

items.question: What do you see as the biggest pressures facing gaming companies and studios today?
items.object: The gaming industry's downturn and need to reduce production costs
items.answer: I think the entire gaming industry has been contracting over the past two years. Although it is a huge market of nearly US$300 billion, you have also seen plenty of layoffs in the industry recently. Everyone is busy cutting costs and improving efficiency, raising prices, and remastering and rereleasing old games. The entire gaming industry is struggling now. There are many reasons, including short-video social-media platforms like TikTok taking away the time people used to spend playing games. Many people would rather scroll short videos than play games. That is one reason. Another is that the industry has not seen a new kind of gameplay like PUBG and battle royale emerge for a long time. As for business models, free-to-play may be a good business model people have discovered recently, but no new business model has emerged either. Meanwhile, overall production costs keep rising. Look at GTA: its production cycle is ten years, and it takes so many people to make something like that. But the price cannot be set too high. You might spend US$30 or US$40 to see a movie here, right? It entertains you for two or three hours. But a game might provide 20 hours of playtime, yet it can only sell for US$30 or US$40 too. So this is a pricing challenge. Everyone is watching how the newest version of GTA will be priced. If it can be priced higher, others may dare to price higher too. At the same time, some AAA titles, such as The Witcher, sell at very low prices, so pricing across the whole industry is also challenging. Many, many reasons have put the gaming industry into a downturn cycle. So they very much want to cut costs and improve efficiency, which is why they need things like Meshy.

items.question: How do you think Meshy can become 100 or 1,000 times bigger than it is today?
items.object: Growing Meshy through step-by-step business building
items.answer: I think you do it step by step. Jensen Huang did not imagine, before building CUDA, that one day the company would have a US$4 trillion market cap, right? I think building a business is about constantly challenging yourself, changing and overturning your own understanding, continually asking customers what else they need, solving those problems, and adding some first-principles thinking. Jensen Huang’s thinking was that the world needs more compute. If I have something that can give you more compute and is programmable, then people will try it and see what problems it can solve. items.question: How do you approach pursuing an ambitious goal before you have figured out how to achieve it?

items.answer: I think one thing that makes me different from others is that I am very biased for action. If there is something I want to do, I do it immediately. I will do it even if I do not sleep at night. Often, when I want to do something, I think about it at night—even though it may still be far from taking shape. It is a little like Elon Musk building rockets: before he had even finished building the rocket engine, he was already thinking about what we would eat on Mars. items.question: What do you see as the most important principle for making a technology startup sustainable?
items.object: Commercial sustainability and the technology R&D flywheel at a startup
items.answer: Thinking about it now, the things Taichi did in its first two years were not entirely without gains; they were just not commercially sustainable. I think the most important thing for a startup is to find a mature monetization or cash-generating model that lets it operate sustainably on its own. The biggest principle is that the technology or product you build must be commercializable. If a technology cannot be commercialized, you cannot use the revenue from commercialization to support future technical research. The technology itself becomes a fireworks show: once the fireworks are over, it is gone. But you want to turn technology R&D into a market—right, a flywheel. You build good technology, which yields a good product; a good product generates good revenue; good revenue attracts good people; good people build good technology. That keeps turning and turning, and that is how you make the company bigger and bigger. But figuring out that pattern is difficult, especially when there is uncertainty.

items.question: How do you describe Andy Grove and Gordon Moore's way of reconsidering Intel's direction when its DRAM business could no longer compete?
items.object: Andy Grove and Gordon Moore's reconsideration of Intel's business direction
items.answer: I'll tell the story. Around 1970, the entire U.S. semiconductor industry was facing a huge challenge. At the time they mainly made DRAM, and Japan had engineers who were hardworking, had great service attitudes, worked overtime, and several companies joined forces to do it together. Intel's DRAM basically could no longer sell; it simply could not compete with Japanese products. Gordon Moore—the Moore behind Moore's Law—and Andy Grove were talking in the office. Andy Grove wrote books such as Only the Paranoid Survive and High Output Management; they are all very good books. They were talking: What should we do? The company was about to become unsustainable, because our DRAM had been completely beaten by the Japanese. Andy Grove said, “If this continues, the board will definitely fire us.” You know, boards in America have a lot of power; they can replace the CEO. Andy Grove said, “Okay, if this continues, the board will definitely fire us, so why don't we fire ourselves—walk out of this room and walk back in? Then let's think: if we were the new CEOs of this company, what would we do?” They concluded that if the company hired a new CEO, they would make CPUs.

items.question: Why do you think Meshy’s remaining technical challenges are solvable?
items.object: Technological progress and Meshy’s remaining technical challenges
items.answer: I think the remaining 50% is solvable. The biggest thing I have learned is: do not underestimate the speed of technological progress. When we first made Mesh, the technology we used was very poor, very old, but we kept iterating. The problems we can solve now are vastly greater than before. At first it could only be used for horror games. Why? Because every model we generated had four faces. Why did they all have four faces? Because after generating the model, our texturing generated one texture each for the front, back, left, and right, and applied them to the model. So on a character's head, you would see one face on the front, one on the side, one on the back—four faces in total. Only horror games could use assets like that. But now we have seen some AA studios, and even some AAA studios, use Meshy for prototypes. As the technology keeps evolving, the opportunity is extremely large. And even today, we may have solved only 5% of the market's niche scenarios; there is still a huge amount of room ahead.

items.question: How has your view of being liked by everyone changed as a leader?
items.object: Being liked by everyone as a leadership priority
items.answer: Perhaps the biggest thing I changed my mind about was that I once very much wanted everyone to like me. I wanted everyone who talked about me to think, “Wow, Yue Ming is a very nice person, Yue Ming is very kind, Yue Ming is a very good friend.” But after experiencing many things, I found that if your goal at work is to make everyone like you, you will ultimately be disliked by everyone. So I no longer pursue being liked by everyone. I pursue being liked by the people who matter. If unimportant people criticize you or think whatever about you, it is fine as long as you believe what you are doing is right. Someone will always criticize you. Another point is looking at the whole team from a manager's perspective. Is a good leader necessarily one everyone likes? Not necessarily. A good leader may be one everyone respects, but not necessarily one everyone likes. Yet people are still willing to follow them. Why? Because they can grow there and do what they want to do. If being liked by everyone becomes your top decision-making priority, it often leads to bad decisions.

items.question: How do you decide whether a startup opportunity is right for you?
items.object: Choosing a startup opportunity
items.answer: Once something becomes consensus and you start doing it, you basically no longer have an opportunity, unless you have ten times others' resources. Big companies can catch up as late movers by pouring in resources. Another question is whether you are genuinely interested in it. That is also worth considering. Liking it or not is the question of whether you want to do it. I think when choosing something to do, you have to consider whether you want to do it, whether you can do it, and timing. There are too many hardworking people in this world; the person who ultimately wins must be the most hardworking one. What determines whether you work hard? Your physical condition, certainly—though that is luck: your genes and upbringing determine whether you can work sixteen, twelve, or eight hours a day. What stage of life are you in? Do you have a family, or do you just want to lie flat now, which is fine? Then lie flat; that is okay. But you have to happen to encounter an opportunity during the period when you are willing to strive. That is time, timing, and luck. With those conditions, if it is a time in which you want to strive, you have the prerequisites for starting a business. You need to be healthy and your family situation needs to be relatively stable. You cannot say you have parents to care for and children to raise, then start a company and expect to balance it easily. At least you cannot do an intense startup; you can start one at lower intensity. If you start up in AI, you must be prepared for a 24/7 job; you must always be on call. After that, I think you need to find an intersection between what you want to do and a large market.

If you are completely unsuited to it—if what you studied, your network, and your experience have absolutely nothing to do with what you are doing—then the chance of success is very low. items.question: How do you think about the relationship between effort and reward in entrepreneurship?
items.object: Effort and reward in entrepreneurship
items.answer: If you believe harmful old sayings such as “you reap what you sow,” I think that is completely deceptive. “Heaven rewards diligence”—I think that is deceptive too. If you believe, “I have worked so hard, so I will definitely be rewarded,” that is completely illogical. The overwhelming majority of effort in the world has no return at all. The bigger the thing you do, the greater the risk; often you put in ninety-nine parts of effort and get no return at all. But your mind protects itself: “I worked so hard—how could there be no return? I must have improved a little, at least.” Once you think like that, you are not facing facts objectively. The harshest fact of entrepreneurship is that most of your effort is useless. But you must make that effort, because you do not know which one part of your hundred parts of effort will be useful. You must therefore try the other ninety-nine, but you must also respect the fact that most of your attempts are of little use.

items.question: How do you see the opportunities and challenges of building Meshy in today's generative AI era?

items.answer: There are many opportunities. Technologically, many techniques have gradually matured—Diffusion, RF, DiT, and MoE—which make building such models possible. items.question: How do you experience the demands of being a CEO compared with doing your PhD?
items.object: The demands and personal growth of entrepreneurship compared with PhD life
items.answer: Being a CEO is more exhausting, of course. My PhD was great. After I changed advisors, my PhD was the happiest time, because I only had to take care of myself. But now, as CEO, my responsibilities are enormous: the company has to win, everyone has to be fed, investors expect the company to grow quickly, and customers want me to deliver new products as soon as possible. As the company grows, there are also many things I am not good at handling that I must now learn to handle. So honestly it is quite tiring, but every day I wake up feeling that the day is good enough and I can energetically meet new challenges. Every one or two months, I feel I have improved again. This process has repaired many flaws in my personality and many blind spots in my understanding. There is a saying I find interesting: in peacetime, nothing trains a person more than entrepreneurship.

items.question: How do you think company culture should serve a business?
items.object: Company culture and winning
items.answer: I think a company's culture always serves winning. If a company's culture prevents it from winning, we should abandon that culture. That does not mean adopting some wolf-like culture or things people dislike. Rather, you should find cultural common ground that a small group of people identify with. It can mean working hard, being responsible, pursuing excellence, taking risks, or embracing change. These are only the process. A good culture necessarily nurtures a good company, a good talent pipeline, and good products. But as CEO, I must choose a culture that can win. If I choose a losing culture, I need not be CEO.

items.question: How do you understand the transition from what you call “stage one,” where others set your tasks, to “stage two,” where you must set your own direction?
items.object: The transition from stage-one execution to stage-two self-direction
items.answer:
The way I think about stage one and stage two is basically this: stage one solves the question of how, and stage two solves the question of why. In stage one, you have a clear goal; in stage two, you do not. In stage one, it is enough to do your own work well; in stage two, you have to think about what the whole team should do. In stage one, others give you problems; in stage two, you give yourself problems.

For example, as an undergraduate, the important thing is to learn knowledge from books. As a graduate student, you may need to find a good research topic. Graduate study itself also has stage one and stage two: at first, your advisor gives you a topic to research; in the second stage, you must find good topics yourself, because your advisor may not have your frontline feel for the problem and may not know which problem is most important. You can only rely on yourself.

Or say you used to be an individual contributor, an IC, at a big company, without managing a team. You just needed to do tasks assigned by your superiors. Once you become a manager, you must give the organization a vision and design its goals so that it can operate; you face enormous uncertainty. Or you used to be an employee and now start a business. When you worked, all platforms and certainty were provided by the company. Once you start a business, you instantly lose all of that. Everything you do instantly becomes something for which you must figure out repeatability yourself. What you do next depends entirely on your own exploration and the new knowledge you acquire.

These two stages are so different that many people continue using stage-one thinking in stage two. That leads to stage-two disasters. The more successful you are in stage one, the more you often suffer in stage two. Why? Because the skills you need in Phase One and Phase Two are completely different. In Phase One, maybe it is about following orders, grinding for efficiency, continuously honing a specific skill. But in Phase Two, no one is directing you anymore, and efficiency is no longer even something you can talk about, because the metric for efficiency has not even been defined—it cannot be defined. Nor will you have the energy to hone a specific skill like coding, drawing, or some other concrete skill. So you will feel extremely uncomfortable.

If you do not realize, OK, I am in Phase Two now—it is like fighting a boss: you finish one health bar, and now it is transformed and you have to fight the second health bar. If you still fight it the way you fought the first health bar, you will die very quickly, and have to start over.

items.question: How would you advise PhD students to approach the transition from publishing their first papers to pursuing broader research impact?
items.object: The transition from execution to impact in PhD research
items.answer: My advice for Phase One PhD students is: just honestly get your papers published. If you do not have even one paper, do not start talking about how you want to see clearly what the trends in the industry are. Phase One is about grinding on execution. Execute this thing well, publish more papers, get more feedback, gain more knowledge. Then, once you have three or four top-conference papers, you need to start thinking: oh, these papers—I mean, they are all the same thing, one paper, right? How well did it do? How many people cited my work? Which industries were changed? Do these works form a system? Have they become work that everyone recognizes as the best? How many people adopt this—for example, ResNet, that is just a plus sign, right? How many people adopt this plus sign? And are people in other fields using our work? Has it broken out of its circle? Only by grinding crazily in Phase One can you get enough information to take you to Phase Two. But once you are in Phase Two, execution is still important, but you need to spend time thinking about why. A lot of people, even in Phase Two, are still churning out filler. They are still like, oh, I have three papers now, and I will publish three more this year, making six. You can certainly keep doing that, but as you just said, a lot of things with 10x impact only require twice as much lazy work.

items.question: How do you distinguish temporary setbacks from real failure when pursuing innovation?
items.object: Failure in innovation
items.answer: I think that a lot of the time, what happens if you fail? People often imagine the consequences of failure to be extremely serious. If I fail, will I die? Will I lose the opportunity to do things in the future? As long as I am alive, I do not think I have failed. And even if your company fails, I would not kill myself or anything. As long as I can stay alive, I can keep making new things. So any failure is only temporary failure. The real failure may be making one or two attempts, then becoming unwilling to innovate again. Once bitten by a snake, you fear a rope for ten years—honestly doing only very conservative things. I think that is the real failure. If your goal is innovation, then since it is innovation, most innovations do not make sense. If it is something that is guaranteed to succeed, then do not innovate. If one out of ten innovations succeeds, that is already pretty good. I often comfort our team members by saying, hey, it is fine if this experiment failed. You just need to have worked hard, and your insight was right. Failure is completely normal, an everyday occurrence. It is so easy to fail.

items.question: Why do you think it is important to keep writing code as a CEO?
items.object: Writing code as a CEO
items.answer: Last week I may have coded for a few hours, two or three hours. Probably less this week, but this week I helped the two students sitting here debug and fixed a bug by reading their code. Maybe 10% of my time goes to that, because you still need to occasionally sample what the current problems actually look like. That is very helpful for hiring and for your technical decisions. If a CEO does not write code, it is very easy to become detached from reality. You think, oh, this problem is easy to solve. But when you look every day at the shitty problems people are solving, you realize, oh, this is actually pretty complicated.

items.question: Why would you worry about no longer writing code as a founder?
items.object: A founder’s hands-on understanding of technology
items.answer: I would worry, because then I would be completely out of touch with the ground, and the decisions I make would all be these high-level, yin-yang-and-five-elements, who-knows-what decisions. I still believe a good founder must be hands-on. Look at Lei Jun, Jason, Elon—they are all very hands-on. Right, they do not necessarily write code, right? They can design products. They can personally negotiate with suppliers; they can have a deep understanding of technology. I think maybe the term hands-on is not quite right. Maybe it is really understanding technology—really understanding technology. I think of Lisa Su, the CEO of AMD. She is in the building next to ours. She said that once, when she gave a talk at MIT—because she graduated from MIT—she said that her biggest advantage over those MBAs was that she actually understands how technology works. She actually understands how technology works, and that is very helpful for many of your business decisions.

items.question: What level of technical understanding do you think you need to lead a technical team?
items.object: Firsthand technical experience as a foundation for leading a technical team
items.answer: I think you have to have done it firsthand at least. For example, if you are doing this Masher thing, you yourself have trained models, trained GANs, trained these CNNs and so on. You may not have trained diffusion, but you roughly know training dynamics and what the alpha and beta parameters in the Adam optimizer are about. If you write compilers and are setting up a compiler team, you should at least have written assembly and written a compiler before. If not, why should anyone else work for you? items.question: Why do you want to make a remastered edition of your Games 201 simulation lectures?
items.object: A remastered edition of his Games 201 simulation lectures
items.answer: Back then I was like you all: interning at NVIDIA. I remember that because of COVID, I was interning remotely in Boston. I remember starting the lectures at 8 a.m., which happened to be 8 p.m. in China. I would lecture from 8 to 9, then sleep again until 12, and then start work at NVIDIA when it was 9 a.m. on the West Coast. Basically, I had no time at all to rest on weekends, and the preparation was extremely rushed. I mean, of course, because there were no tutorials on simulation in China at the time, everyone thought it was okay. But I think it was only from 0 to 1; it did not really explain many of the technical details in simulation thoroughly enough, because I had very limited time to prepare. So I still want to do this better.

items.question: What do you think it means to be ready to start a company?
items.object: Readiness to start a company
items.answer: I think first is to get ready. You first need to know whether you are ready for starting a company. Being ready does not mean you have figured out what you will do; rather, you need to be able to bear failure. That includes perhaps your parents being in relatively good health, and you having a stable family, so that you can think 24/7 about how your company should be run. After you have those things in order, action may actually be the most important thing. Take action.

items.question: How do you think about taking the step to start a company before you have much experience or have fully thought it through?
items.object: Taking the step to start a company
items.answer: I mean actually taking that step to start a company. In fact, a lot of things can be learned; you can quickly experiment and learn, then discover that you are a dumbass and become a better version of yourself. So experience is not that important, and neither is whether you have fully thought it through. As long as you can bear the consequences of failure, as long as your mindset is: if it fails, it fails—what can happen? When I started my company, my mindset was, OK, I graduated with my PhD in three and a half years. Even if I wasted two years, that would be the equivalent of graduating in five and a half years. So what? What could happen? That was my mindset at the time. And my parents were still in pretty good health then, and there was nothing in my family that I needed to worry about. So— Once you do it, you do it.
